en: The Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī of the Supreme Intention Spoken by the Buddha,
translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Court Rank of Chao San Dafu, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial,
and Dharma-Transmitting Master, the Subject Shi Hu, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa-candana Vihāra in the city of Kapilavastu,
together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
The eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, stood surrounding him in reverent attendance, gazing up at him.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda and the great assembly, saying:
"I observe this southern continent of Jambudvīpa during the final age."
Because all sentient beings have meager merit,
various malevolent spirits and ghosts arise to instigate calamities and disasters,
harassing and disturbing sentient beings so that they find no peace or stability.
"There is a dhāraṇī capable of pacifying calamities and increasing auspiciousness;
I shall now proclaim it, so listen attentively.
At that time, Ānanda and the great assembly [listened].
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, they listened in silence.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda,
in the past, there was a bhikṣu in this Jambudvīpa."
His name was Enchō.
On the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the ninth month,
while traveling northward at a distance of no more than four *yojanas* from the land of China, he suddenly beheld a divine being standing far off along the way.
This divine being was thirty cubits tall with a face four cubits in circumference.
When the bhikṣu who transmits the teachings saw this divine being,
he observed that his stature was magnificent and his countenance was serene and joyful.
Upon careful and discerning observation, he realized that this was not another person,
but was indeed the true Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta. Thereupon,
the bhikṣu who had transmitted the teachings prostrated before the divine being, touching his five limbs to the ground in reverent salutation.
Having prostrated and risen, he joined his palms, gazed up with reverence, and addressed the divine being, saying:
"Why has the youth Mañjuśrī manifested such a sign?
I now know with certainty that this is surely no other holy one."
Then that divine being addressed the bhikṣu, saying, "It is truly as you say; I am Mañjuśrī.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu who had transmitted the teachings spoke again to the divine being, saying:
"For what reason has this sign appeared today?
Then that divine being said to the bhikṣu Denchō, "Do you not know?"
"Now there shall be calamities in Jambudvīpa in the south.
Sentient beings of meager merit will contract various diseases and undergo manifold sufferings.
A bhikṣu addressed him, saying:
"Now, why has this calamity suddenly occurred in Jambudvīpa in the south?
The divine being replied,
"Now, on the southern side of Mount Sumeru, there is an asura."
Having conceived evil intentions, he led his retinue to demand battle with the gods.
At that time, the asuras obstructed the sun, moon, and stars so that their light did not appear.
Furthermore, there were immeasurable and extremely malevolent yakṣas, gandharvas, garuḍas,
and others dwelling on the southern face of Mount Sumeru;
having seen the asuras manifesting these signs, they likewise joined them in alliance.
At that time, the devas were defeated and the asuras gained the victory.
Then, in Jambudvīpa in the south,
the radiance of the sun, moon, and stars was suddenly seen to be eclipsed.
Various ill-omened signs appeared everywhere;
wind and rain fell out of season, and droughts and floods occurred with great frequency.
The five grains and all crops blossomed but failed to bear fruit.
Even if there were fruits and grains, they would be tasteless;
they would cause the physical strength, vitality, and majestic radiance of all sentient beings to diminish and deteriorate.
Furthermore, there would be various classes of evil spirits dwelling on the earth, such as the piśācas.
They transform their original forms to manifest various strange appearances;
they may take the shape of lions, tigers, or wolves, or assume the likeness of dogs and jackals.
They also manifest the forms of those women to harass and disturb sentient beings.
They cause them to contract various diseases and sufferings,
namely: goiters, wind disorders, phlegm-induced vomiting,
eye diseases, headaches, abdominal pains, and even hemorrhoids and fistulas.
Furthermore, there are malarial fevers—whether occurring daily, every other day, momentarily, or persisting for months—as well as afflictions such as sores, rashes, and scabies;
all manner of evil diseases shall prevail throughout Jambudvīpa.
It causes all sentient beings to undergo extreme suffering and affliction;
among those of meager merit, there is no one who can escape it—
whether they be old, middle-aged, young, or infants.
Because of this pestilence, many have met with untimely death.
Bhikṣus, it is for this reason that I harbor feelings of sorrow and compassion;
therefore, I manifest this appearance to inform people of my knowledge.
"Monks, I now tell you: if there are sentient beings who, for the sake of themselves and their retinues,
even down to their villages and kingdoms,
wish to avert calamities and increase merit and auspiciousness."
First, one should generate deep faith and reverence toward the Triple Gem,
and then prepare offerings of famous flowers, rare fruits, incense for burning, ointments,
and various other ritual implements to perform worship.
One must, with a sincere mind, abstain from food for seven days;
reciting the supreme *mantra* (vidyā) with courageous concentration four times during the day and four times at night, those calamities will certainly be extinguished.
It is able to increase all blessings and auspiciousness.

If a bhikṣu wishes to recite that supreme *mantra*, he must first prostrate and call upon the name of the Tathāgata Vast and Profound Wisdom Roaring King (*Namo Gwang-da Shen-shen Chi-wei Chen-hou Wang Ju-lai*). Only after this should he proceed.
He then recited the dhāraṇī.
At that time, the divine being spoke to the bhikṣu who had transmitted the teaching,
proclaiming the *Paramārthadhāraṇī*, saying:
Tadyathā vibhūtagarjite vibhūtaśvare vibhūtayone svāhā | namo sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhitathāgatāya | tadyathā he...
Āṃ mahi mahāmahi svāhā | Namaḥ guṇakara-sya tathāgatasya | Tadyathā | Gaganakari gaganasambhave gagana-kṛte te svāhā | Namaḥ ratnānām ||
Gata namas tathāgatāya | tadyathā | ratnānudgate ratna-sambhave svāhā | namo mahā-ṛddhi-sarvamaitri-tathāgatāya ||
Tadyathā amā-mahi svāhā | Namo mānasa-tat-sadbhyas tathāgatebhyaḥ | Tadyathā amana-satvaṃ jñāna-padma-sarva-padma-sambhave ||
Rihitakārye svāhā | Namo sarvabuddhabodhisattvānām | Namo āryamañjuśriye | Tadyathā | Jaye jayavati rame ramite mahāramaḥ | svāhā ||
Hīḥ svāhā | Namo ārya-vajracarcikāyai | Tadyathā | Gaganatate gaganavikrānte hīme svāhā | Namo ārya-samanta-...
Tathāgata-tantrajñāna-hīṃ vaṇḍi mahā-vaṇḍi amṛta-vaṇḍi vigatarājaśrī svāhā | Namaḥ... [The remainder of the mantra follows].
*Ṛyavajra-dīpate tata danyatha kṛtite ta sarva-jñāni-pi āti-kṛtite ta sarva-jñāni-pi vajra*...
SAMBHAVE VAJRA-BHĪṢAṆAKĀYA SVĀHĀ | NAMAḤ SARVA-BUDDHA-BODHISATTVĀNĀM TADYATHĀ ŚVETAKARṆE VĀRĀṆIYE SVĀHĀ ||
Sattvānīṃ hana bhañja pūṇḍarīkāya svāhā | mahānte nambanīye svāhā | nuraviṃnurīye svāhā | ravikṛte svāhā | śānte sive ni svāhā ||
Vāpanaye svāhā | Amunadraye karāpase kṛtitaḥ svāhā | Arjanaviddhamanye svāhā | Dantukarye svāhā | Mīgakarye svāhā ||
Mala-vandite svāhā | Mṛdvangane svāhā | Karmasādhanike svāhā | Ekaramaye svāhā | Ayugzariṇye svāhā | Praṇamomi ||
Phaḥ | Yutaḥ | Svāhā sarvakalmaṣavaraṇaniḥśeṣitāya svāhā | Sarvabuddha-niḥśeṣitāya svāhā | Eka-śīrṣāya svāhā.
*Śvāhā asurebhyaḥ svāhā | bhūtebhyaḥ svāhā | abhūtebhyaḥ svāhā | sarvabhūtagaṇebhyaḥ samaye svāhā | mama sarvānāṃ ca svāhā.* At that time, the divine being spoke this supreme intention.
Having recited the dhāraṇī,
he addressed the bhikṣu who was transmitting the teaching, saying:
"You should now, by means of this dhāraṇī, [spread it] throughout the ten directions within Jambudvīpa in the south."
It shall be proclaimed throughout every kingdom, city,
and village so that all sentient beings may hear and know it,
ensuring that this dhāraṇī is widely disseminated and propagated.
Why is this? Because it enables sentient beings to increase their merit and virtue,
and because it enables sentient beings to eliminate all suffering and affliction.
Because it can eliminate all calamities within the world;
because it can cause malevolent spirits and deities to cease their evil intentions;
and because it can cause the kings, ministers, and subjects in whatever kingdoms, cities, towns, or villages it reaches [to attain peace].
Because all shall attain peace, security, and happiness. Bhikṣus,
if there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to reverently make offerings to, uphold, read, and recite this dhāraṇī...
To pacify calamities and increase merit and virtue,
one should give rise to a heart of utmost sincerity and take refuge in the Triple Gem.
For a period of seven days and seven nights, one should daily prepare various incenses, flowers, food, and drink to make offerings to the Buddha.
Furthermore, he provided for seven monks daily.
Then, at midnight, in his own courtyard,
he lit a great torch to provide illumination and recited this dhāraṇī.
One shall attain liberation from all calamities.
If a bhikṣu, or a son or daughter of good family, is able to act in this manner,
they shall attain liberation for themselves.
If a bhikṣu, during the second seven-day period, likewise prepares various kinds of incense, flowers, food, and drink,
making offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha with double the intensity as before,
then all that person’s parents will likewise attain liberation.
If a bhikṣu, during the three seven-day periods, can thus redouble his previous efforts toward the Buddha, Dharma,
and Saṅgha by reverently making offerings of various incenses, flowers, food, and drink, [he shall attain such merit].
That person’s sons, daughters, and all their retinue shall likewise attain liberation.
If a bhikṣu practices in this manner for four seven-day periods,
redoubling his diligence and devotion compared to before without slackening, [the same result shall follow].
All the people dwelling in the village where that person resides shall all attain liberation.
To speak briefly, monks, this surpasses the previous offerings made to the Buddha,
Dharma, and Sangha for as many as seven weeks, with each successive week being many times superior to the one before.
The merit obtained by that person shall extend upward to the king and downward to the common people;
throughout the realm, all shall universally attain liberation.
"Monks, you should know that I now tell you this:
you must uphold this Dharma in this world and in other realms,
and quickly proclaim it so that it may spread far and wide."
Why is this? Because it is able to eliminate the various kinds of suffering and affliction for sentient beings,
and to increase their various kinds of merit and virtue.
Furthermore, monks, if there are those who hear this Dharma and recognize its benefits, yet do not revere it in their hearts;
nor can they explain it extensively for others,
nor can they themselves diligently recite and study it.
"Monks, you should know that such a person incurs the fault of concealing the Dharma,
which is equal to the five heinous crimes. If there are sentient beings who hear this Dharma,
they shall not disobey my teaching but shall personally rely upon the Dharma."
One should uphold, recite, and pay homage to it with reverence;
furthermore, one should cultivate merit for others according to the Dharma and be able to disseminate it widely to benefit all sentient beings.
“Bhikṣu, I immediately knew from afar that I had previously gone to Mount Sumeru for this person’s sake;
I went to the abodes of the devas, asuras, gandharvas, and garuḍas,
and with a mind of benefit, I subdued and exhorted them.”
He preached the Dharma for them, causing them all to rejoice;
he caused those devas, humans, asuras,
and others to cease their contentious minds and to respect one another.
Immediately, the calamities within the realm of Jambudvīpa were extinguished and pestilence did not arise;
all malevolent spirits each went into hiding,
and all sentient beings attained peace and happiness.
When that divine being had finished speaking these matters, he vanished from sight.
The bhikṣu who had received the teaching followed and upheld what was transmitted.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
In a past life, that youth Mañjuśrī,
through the power of skillful means, taught such a Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
I shall now proclaim it once again for you.
May you single-mindedly uphold, receive, read, and recite it,
so that in future ages it may be widely disseminated,
eliminating calamities and increasing auspiciousness.
Then Ānanda and the great assembly,
having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all filled with joy;
they received and upheld it with single-minded devotion, prostrated before the Buddha, and withdrew.
The Sūtra on the Dhāraṇī of the Supreme Intention Spoken by the Buddha.
